{{Short description|Space where bounded operators are continuous}}
In [[mathematics]], particularly in [[functional analysis]], a '''bornological space''' is a type of space which, in some sense, possesses the minimum amount of structure needed to address questions of boundedness of [[Bounded set (topological vector space)|sets]] and [[Bounded linear operator|linear maps]], in the same way that a [[topological space]] possesses the minimum amount of structure needed to address questions of [[Continuous map (topology)|continuity]]. 
Bornological spaces are distinguished by the property that a linear map from a bornological space into any [[Locally convex topological vector space|locally convex]] spaces is continuous if and only if it is a [[bounded linear operator]].

Bornological spaces were first studied by [[George Mackey]].{{fact|date=December 2022}} The name was coined by [[Nicolas Bourbaki|Bourbaki]]{{fact|date=December 2022}} after {{wikt-lang|fr|borné}}, the French word for "[[bounded set|bounded]]".

==Bornologies and bounded maps==
{{Main|Bornology}}

A '''{{em|bornology}}''' on a set <math>X</math> is a collection <math>\mathcal{B}</math> of subsets of <math>X</math> that satisfy all the following conditions:
<ol>
<li><math>\mathcal{B}</math> covers <math>X;</math> that is, <math>X = \cup \mathcal{B}</math>;</li>
<li><math>\mathcal{B}</math> is stable under inclusions; that is, if <math>B \in \mathcal{B}</math> and <math>A \subseteq B,</math> then <math>A \in \mathcal{B}</math>;</li>
<li><math>\mathcal{B}</math> is stable under finite unions; that is,  if <math>B_1, \ldots, B_n \in \mathcal{B}</math> then <math>B_1 \cup \cdots \cup B_n \in \mathcal{B}</math>;</li>
</ol>
Elements of the collection <math>\mathcal{B}</math> are called '''{{em|<math>\mathcal{B}</math>-bounded}}''' or simply '''{{em|bounded sets}}''' if <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is understood.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|p=168}} 
The pair <math>(X, \mathcal{B})</math> is called a '''{{em|bounded structure}}''' or a '''{{em|bornological set}}'''.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|p=168}}

A '''{{em|base}}''' or '''{{em|fundamental system}}''' of a bornology <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is a subset <math>\mathcal{B}_0</math> of <math>\mathcal{B}</math> such that each element of <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is a subset of some element of <math>\mathcal{B}_0.</math> Given a collection <math>\mathcal{S}</math> of subsets of <math>X,</math> the smallest bornology containing <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is called the '''{{em|bornology generated by <math>\mathcal{S}.</math>}}'''{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=156–175}}

If <math>(X, \mathcal{B})</math> and <math>(Y, \mathcal{C})</math> are bornological sets then their '''{{em|product bornology}}''' on <math>X \times Y</math> is the bornology having as a base the collection of all sets of the form <math>B \times C,</math> where <math>B \in \mathcal{B}</math> and <math>C \in \mathcal{C}.</math>{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=156–175}} 
A subset of <math>X \times Y</math> is bounded in the product bornology if and only if its image under the canonical projections onto <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are both bounded. 

===Bounded maps===

If <math>(X, \mathcal{B})</math> and <math>(Y, \mathcal{C})</math> are bornological sets then a function <math>f : X \to Y</math> is said to be a '''{{em|locally bounded map}}''' or a '''{{em|bounded map}}''' (with respect to these bornologies) if it maps <math>\mathcal{B}</math>-bounded subsets of <math>X</math> to <math>\mathcal{C}</math>-bounded subsets of <math>Y;</math> that is, if <math>f(\mathcal{B}) \subseteq \mathcal{C}.</math>{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=156–175}} 
If in addition <math>f</math> is a bijection and <math>f^{-1}</math> is also bounded then <math>f</math> is called a '''{{em|bornological isomorphism}}'''.

== Vector bornologies ==
{{Main|Vector bornology}}

Let <math>X</math> be a vector space over a [[Field (mathematics)|field]] <math>\mathbb{K}</math> where <math>\mathbb{K}</math> has a bornology <math>\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{K}}.</math> 
A bornology <math>\mathcal{B}</math> on <math>X</math> is called a '''{{em|vector bornology on <math>X</math>}}''' if it is stable under vector addition, scalar multiplication, and the formation of [[balanced hull]]s (i.e. if the sum of two bounded sets is bounded, etc.).

If <math>X</math> is a [[topological vector space]] (TVS) and <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is a bornology on <math>X,</math> then the following are equivalent: 
<ol>
<li><math>\mathcal{B}</math> is a vector bornology;</li>
<li>Finite sums and balanced hulls of <math>\mathcal{B}</math>-bounded sets are <math>\mathcal{B}</math>-bounded;{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=156–175}}</li>
<li>The scalar multiplication map <math>\mathbb{K} \times X \to X</math> defined by <math>(s, x) \mapsto sx</math> and the addition map <math>X \times X \to X</math> defined by <math>(x, y) \mapsto x + y,</math> are both bounded when their domains carry their product bornologies (i.e. they map bounded subsets to bounded subsets).{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=156–175}}</li>
</ol>

A vector bornology <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is called a {{em|'''convex vector bornology'''}} if it is stable under the formation of [[convex hull]]s (i.e. the convex hull of a bounded set is bounded) then <math>\mathcal{B}.</math> 
And a vector bornology <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is called {{em|'''separated'''}} if the only bounded vector subspace of <math>X</math> is the 0-dimensional trivial space <math>\{ 0 \}.</math> 

Usually, <math>\mathbb{K}</math> is either the real or complex numbers, in which case a vector bornology <math>\mathcal{B}</math> on <math>X</math> will be called a '''{{em|convex vector bornology}}''' if <math>\mathcal{B}</math> has a base consisting of [[Convex set|convex]] sets. 

=== Bornivorous subsets ===

A subset <math>A</math> of <math>X</math> is called '''{{em|[[bornivorous]]}}''' and a '''{{em|bornivore}}''' if it [[absorbing set|absorbs]] every bounded set.

In a vector bornology, <math>A</math> is bornivorous if it absorbs every bounded balanced set and in a convex vector bornology <math>A</math> is bornivorous if it absorbs every bounded disk.

Two TVS topologies on the same vector space have that same bounded subsets if and only if they have the same bornivores.{{sfn|Wilansky|2013|p=50}}

Every bornivorous subset of a locally convex [[metrizable topological vector space]] is a neighborhood of the origin.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}

==== Mackey convergence ====

A sequence <math>x_\bull = (x_i)_{i=1}^\infty</math> in a TVS <math>X</math> is said to be {{em|'''Mackey convergent''' to <math>0</math>}} if there exists a sequence of positive real numbers <math>r_\bull = (r_i)_{i=1}^\infty</math> diverging to <math>\infty</math> such that <math>(r_i x_i)_{i=1}^\infty</math> converges to <math>0</math> in <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Swartz|1992|pp=15–16}}

=== Bornology of a topological vector space ===

Every [[topological vector space]] <math>X,</math> at least on a non discrete [[valued field]] gives a bornology on <math>X</math> by defining a subset <math>B \subseteq X</math> to be [[Bounded set (topological vector space)|bounded]] (or von-Neumann bounded), if and only if for all open sets <math>U \subseteq X</math> containing zero there exists a <math>r > 0</math> with <math>B \subseteq rU.</math> 
If <math>X</math> is a [[Locally convex topological vector space|locally convex]] [[topological vector space]] then <math>B \subseteq X</math> is bounded if and only if all continuous semi-norms on <math>X</math> are bounded on <math>B.</math>

The set of all [[Bounded set (topological vector space)|bounded]] subsets of a topological vector space <math>X</math> is called '''{{em|the bornology}}''' or '''{{em|the von Neumann bornology}}''' of <math>X.</math>

If <math>X</math> is a [[locally convex topological vector space]], then an [[Absorbing set|absorbing]] [[Absolutely convex set|disk]] <math>D</math> in <math>X</math> is bornivorous (resp. infrabornivorous) if and only if its [[Minkowski functional]] is locally bounded (resp. infrabounded).{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}

=== Induced topology ===

If <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is a convex vector bornology on a vector space <math>X,</math> then the collection <math>\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{B}}(0)</math> of all convex [[Balanced set|balanced]] subsets of <math>X</math> that are bornivorous forms a [[neighborhood basis]] at the origin for a [[Locally convex topological vector space|locally convex]] topology on <math>X</math> called the '''{{em|topology induced by <math>\mathcal{B}</math>}}'''.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}

If <math>(X, \tau)</math> is a TVS then the '''{{em|bornological space associated with <math>X</math>}}''' is the vector space <math>X</math> endowed with the locally convex topology induced by the von Neumann bornology of <math>(X, \tau).</math>{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}|math_statement=
Let <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> be locally convex TVS and let <math>X_b</math> denote <math>X</math> endowed with the topology induced by von Neumann bornology of <math>X.</math> Define <math>Y_b</math> similarly. Then a linear map <math>L : X \to Y</math> is a bounded linear operator if and only if <math>L : X_b \to Y</math> is continuous.

Moreover, if <math>X</math> is bornological, <math>Y</math> is Hausdorff, and <math>L : X \to Y</math> is continuous linear map then so is <math>L : X \to Y_b.</math> If in addition <math>X</math> is also ultrabornological, then the continuity of <math>L : X \to Y</math> implies the continuity of <math>L : X \to Y_{ub},</math> where <math>Y_{ub}</math> is the ultrabornological space associated with <math>Y.</math> 
}}

== Quasi-bornological spaces ==

Quasi-bornological spaces where introduced by S. Iyahen in 1968.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=453–454}}

A [[topological vector space]] (TVS) <math>(X, \tau)</math> with a [[continuous dual]] <math>X^{\prime}</math> is called a '''{{em|quasi-bornological space}}'''{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=453–454}} if any of the following equivalent conditions holds:

<ol>
<li>Every [[bounded linear operator]] from <math>X</math> into another TVS is [[Continuous linear operator|continuous]].{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=453–454}}</li>
<li>Every bounded linear operator from <math>X</math> into a [[F-space|complete metrizable TVS]] is continuous.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=453–454}}{{sfn|Adasch|Ernst|Keim|1978|pp=60–61}}</li>
<li>Every knot in a bornivorous string is a neighborhood of the origin.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=453–454}}</li>
</ol>

Every [[Metrizable topological vector space|pseudometrizable TVS]] is quasi-bornological. {{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=453–454}} 
A TVS <math>(X, \tau)</math> in which every [[bornivorous set]] is a neighborhood of the origin is a quasi-bornological space.{{sfn|Wilansky|2013|p=48}} 
If <math>X</math> is a quasi-bornological TVS then the finest locally convex topology on <math>X</math> that is coarser than <math>\tau</math> makes <math>X</math> into a locally convex bornological space.

=== Bornological space ===

In functional analysis, a [[locally convex topological vector space]] is a bornological space if its topology can be recovered from its bornology in a natural way.

Every locally convex quasi-bornological space is bornological but there exist bornological spaces that are {{em|not}} quasi-bornological.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=453–454}}

A [[topological vector space]] (TVS) <math>(X, \tau)</math> with a [[continuous dual]] <math>X^{\prime}</math> is called a '''{{em|bornological space}}''' if it is locally convex and any of the following equivalent conditions holds:

<ol>
<li>Every convex, balanced, and bornivorous set in <math>X</math> is a neighborhood of zero.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
<li>Every [[bounded linear operator]] from <math>X</math> into a locally convex TVS is [[Continuous linear operator|continuous]].{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}
* Recall that a linear map is bounded if and only if it maps any sequence converging to <math>0</math> in the domain to a bounded subset of the codomain.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}} In particular, any linear map that is sequentially continuous at the origin is bounded.</li>
<li>Every bounded linear operator from <math>X</math> into a [[seminormed space]] is continuous.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
<li>Every bounded linear operator from <math>X</math> into a [[Banach space]] is continuous.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
</ol>

If <math>X</math> is a [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[locally convex space]] then we may add to this list:{{sfn|Adasch|Ernst|Keim|1978|pp=60–61}}
<ol start=5>
<li>The locally convex topology [[#Induced topology|induced by]] the von Neumann bornology on <math>X</math> is the same as <math>\tau,</math> <math>X</math>'s given topology.</li>
<li>Every bounded [[seminorm]] on <math>X</math> is continuous.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
<li>Any other Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space topology on <math>X</math> that has the same (von&nbsp;Neumann) bornology as <math>(X, \tau)</math> is necessarily coarser than <math>\tau.</math></li>
<li><math>X</math> is the inductive limit of normed spaces.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
<li><math>X</math> is the inductive limit of the normed spaces <math>X_D</math> as <math>D</math> varies over the closed and bounded disks of <math>X</math> (or as <math>D</math> varies over the bounded disks of <math>X</math>).{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
<li><math>X</math> carries the Mackey topology <math>\tau(X, X^{\prime})</math> and all bounded linear functionals on <math>X</math> are continuous.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
<li>
<math>X</math> has both of the following properties:
* <math>X</math> is '''{{em|convex-sequential}}''' or '''{{em|C-sequential}}''', which means that every convex sequentially open subset of <math>X</math> is open,
* <math>X</math> is '''{{em|sequentially bornological}}''' or '''{{em|S-bornological}}''', which means that every convex and bornivorous subset of <math>X</math> is sequentially open.
where a subset <math>A</math> of <math>X</math> is called '''{{em|[[Sequential space|sequentially open]]}}''' if every sequence converging to <math>0</math> eventually belongs to <math>A.</math>
</li>
</ol>

Every sequentially continuous linear operator from a locally convex bornological space into a locally convex TVS is continuous,{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}} where recall that a linear operator is sequentially continuous if and only if it is sequentially continuous at the origin. 
Thus for linear maps from a bornological space into a locally convex space, continuity is equivalent to sequential continuity at the origin. More generally, we even have the following:

<ul>
<li>Any linear map <math>F : X \to Y</math> from a locally convex bornological space into a locally convex space <math>Y</math> that maps null sequences in <math>X</math> to [[Bounded set (topological vector space)|bounded subsets]] of <math>Y</math> is necessarily continuous.</li>
</ul>

=== Sufficient conditions ===

{{Math theorem|name=Mackey–Ulam theorem{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|p=450}}|math_statement=
The product of a collection <math>X_\bull = ( X_i)_{i \in I}</math> locally convex bornological spaces is bornological if and only if <math>I</math> does {{em|not}} admit an [[Ulam measure]].
}}

As a consequent of the Mackey–Ulam theorem, "for all practical purposes, the product of bornological spaces 
is bornological."{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|p=450}}

The following topological vector spaces are all bornological:
<ul>
<li>Any locally convex [[Metrizable topological vector space|pseudometrizable TVS]] is bornological.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}{{sfn|Adasch|Ernst|Keim|1978|pp=60–65}} 
* Thus every [[normed space]] and [[Fréchet space]] is bornological.</li>
<li>Any strict inductive limit of bornological spaces, in particular any [[LF-space|strict ''LF''-space]], is bornological.
* This shows that there are bornological spaces that are not metrizable.</li>
<li>A countable product of locally convex bornological spaces is bornological.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|p=453}}{{sfn|Adasch|Ernst|Keim|1978|pp=60–65}}</li>
<li>Quotients of Hausdorff locally convex bornological spaces are bornological.{{sfn|Adasch|Ernst|Keim|1978|pp=60–65}}</li>
<li>The direct sum and inductive limit of Hausdorff locally convex bornological spaces is bornological.{{sfn|Adasch|Ernst|Keim|1978|pp=60–65}}</li>
<li>[[Fréchet space|Fréchet]] [[Montel space|Montel]] spaces have bornological [[Strong dual space|strong duals]].</li>
<li>The strong dual of every [[reflexive space|reflexive]] [[Fréchet space]] is bornological.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|p=144}}</li>
<li>If the strong dual of a metrizable locally convex space is [[Separable space|separable]], then it is bornological.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|p=144}}</li>
<li>A vector subspace of a Hausdorff locally convex bornological space <math>X</math> that has finite codimension in <math>X</math> is bornological.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}{{sfn|Adasch|Ernst|Keim|1978|pp=60–65}}</li>
<li>The [[Locally convex topological vector space|finest locally convex topology]] on a vector space is bornological.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
</ul>

;Counterexamples

There exists a bornological [[LB-space]] whose strong bidual is {{em|not}} bornological.{{sfn|Khaleelulla|1982|pp=28–63}} 

A closed vector subspace of a locally convex bornological space is not necessarily bornological.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=103–110}} 
There exists a closed vector subspace of a locally convex bornological space that is complete (and so sequentially complete) but neither barrelled nor bornological.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}} 

Bornological spaces need not be [[Barrelled space|barrelled]] and barrelled spaces need not be bornological.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}} Because every locally convex ultrabornological space is barrelled,{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}} it follows that a bornological space is not necessarily ultrabornological.

=== Properties ===

<ul>
<li>The [[strong dual space]] of a locally convex bornological space is [[Complete topological vector space|complete]].{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
<li>Every locally convex bornological space is [[Infrabarreled space|infrabarrelled]].{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
<li>Every Hausdorff sequentially complete bornological TVS is [[Ultrabornological space|ultrabornological]].{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}
* Thus every [[Complete topological vector space|complete]] Hausdorff bornological space is ultrabornological.
* In particular, every [[Fréchet space]] is ultrabornological.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
<li>The finite product of locally convex ultrabornological spaces is ultrabornological.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
<li>Every Hausdorff bornological space is [[quasi-barrelled]].{{sfn|Adasch|Ernst|Keim|1978|pp=70–73}}</li>
<li>Given a bornological space <math>X</math> with [[continuous dual]] <math>X^{\prime},</math> the topology of <math>X</math> coincides with the [[Mackey topology]] <math>\tau(X, X^{\prime}).</math> 
* In particular, bornological spaces are [[Mackey space]]s.</li>
<li>Every [[quasi-complete]] (i.e. all closed and bounded subsets are complete) bornological space is [[Barrelled space|barrelled]]. There exist, however, bornological spaces that are not barrelled.</li>
<li>Every bornological space is the inductive limit of normed spaces (and Banach spaces if the space is also quasi-complete).</li>
<li>
Let <math>X</math> be a metrizable locally convex space with continuous dual <math>X^{\prime}.</math> Then the following are equivalent:
<ol>
<li><math>\beta(X^{\prime}, X)</math> is bornological.</li>
<li><math>\beta(X^{\prime}, X)</math> is [[barrelled space|quasi-barrelled]].</li>
<li><math>\beta(X^{\prime}, X)</math> is [[barrelled space|barrelled]].</li>
<li><math>X</math> is a [[distinguished space]].</li>
</ol>
</li>
<li>If <math>L : X \to Y</math> is a linear map between locally convex spaces and if <math>X</math> is bornological, then the following are equivalent:
<ol>
<li><math>L : X \to Y</math> is continuous.</li>
<li><math>L : X \to Y</math> is sequentially continuous.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
<li>For every set <math>B \subseteq X</math> that's bounded in <math>X,</math> <math>L(B)</math> is bounded.</li>
<li>If <math>x_{\bull} = (x_i)_{i=1}^\infty</math> is a null sequence in <math>X</math> then <math>L \circ x_\bull = (L(x_i))_{i=1}^\infty</math> is a null sequence in <math>Y.</math></li>
<li>If <math>x_\bull = (x_i)_{i=1}^\infty</math> is a Mackey convergent null sequence in <math>X</math> then <math>L \circ x_\bull = (L(x_i))_{i=1}^\infty </math> is a bounded subset of <math>Y.</math></li>
</ol>
</li>
<li>Suppose that <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are [[locally convex]] TVSs and that the space of continuous linear maps <math>L_b(X; Y)</math> is endowed with the [[Topologies on spaces of linear maps|topology of uniform convergence on bounded subsets]] of <math>X.</math> If <math>X</math> is a bornological space and if <math>Y</math> is [[Complete topological vector space|complete]] then <math>L_b(X; Y)</math> is a complete TVS.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}
* In particular, the strong dual of a locally convex bornological space is complete.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}} However, it need not be bornological.</li>
</ul>

;Subsets

<ul>
<li>In a locally convex bornological space, every convex bornivorous set <math>B</math> is a neighborhood of <math>0</math> (<math>B</math> is {{em|not}} required to be a disk).{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
<li>Every bornivorous subset of a locally convex [[metrizable topological vector space]] is a neighborhood of the origin.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
<li>Closed vector subspaces of bornological space need not be bornological.{{sfn|Narici|Beckenstein|2011|pp=441–457}}</li>
</ul>

== Ultrabornological spaces ==
{{Main|Ultrabornological space}}

A disk in a topological vector space <math>X</math> is called '''{{em|infrabornivorous}}''' if it absorbs all [[Banach disk]]s.

If <math>X</math> is locally convex and Hausdorff, then a disk is infrabornivorous if and only if it absorbs all compact disks.

A locally convex space is called '''{{em|ultrabornological}}''' if any of the following equivalent conditions hold:
<ol>
<li>Every infrabornivorous disk is a neighborhood of the origin.</li>
<li><math>X</math> is the inductive limit of the spaces <math>X_D</math> as <math>D</math> varies over all compact disks in <math>X.</math></li>
<li>A [[seminorm]] on <math>X</math> that is bounded on each Banach disk is necessarily continuous.</li>
<li>For every locally convex space <math>Y</math> and every linear map <math>u : X \to Y,</math> if <math>u</math> is bounded on each Banach disk then <math>u</math> is continuous.</li>
<li>For every Banach space <math>Y</math> and every linear map <math>u : X \to Y,</math> if <math>u</math> is bounded on each Banach disk then <math>u</math> is continuous.</li>
</ol>

=== Properties ===

The finite product of ultrabornological spaces is ultrabornological. Inductive limits of ultrabornological spaces are ultrabornological.
